# terraform-provider-developer knowledge log

This is the reinforcement log for the vendor-agnostic base agent
([terraform-provider-developer.agent.md](terraform-provider-developer.agent.md)).
It is **append-only** - never rewrite or delete a prior entry, only add new
ones below. Only genuinely vendor-agnostic findings belong here (a codegen
toolchain quirk, a generic hand-written-CRUD pattern, a portability fix, an
agent/prompt authoring convention). Vendor-specific findings (SDK type
shapes, API behavior, tenant-specific quirks) belong in the relevant vendor
specialist's own knowledge file instead - if you're not sure which file an
entry belongs in, ask: "would this be true for a completely different
vendor's OpenAPI-codegen-based Terraform provider?" If yes, it belongs here.

## Entry Template

```
- Date: YYYY-MM-DD
- Task type: pipeline | author-agent | review
- Target/Scope: <files touched or pipeline stage under discussion>
- Summary: <what was done/found, and why - cite evidence (command output,
  file/line) rather than asserting from memory>
- Delegated to: <specialist agent(s) invoked, or "none">
- Validation: <commands run and outcomes, Phase A / Phase B split if relevant>
- Guardrail update: <new Workflow/Enforcement Rule added, or "none">
```

## Hand-Written CRUD Pattern Catalog

Full writeups, evidence, and gotchas for the hand-written-CRUD sub-patterns
indexed in stage 6 ("Hand-write CRUD") of the base agent's Generic Codegen
Pipeline. Each entry below is the verbatim pattern text relocated out of the
agent file so that file stays a scannable menu; consult the matching entry
here once you have recognized which pattern applies. These are reference
patterns, not dated log entries, so they intentionally do not follow the
Entry Template above.

### Client-provider interface

- A small client-provider interface satisfied by the root provider type, to avoid an import cycle between a per-resource package and the root provider package.

### Error-formatting helper

- A shared error-formatting helper that extracts a useful diagnostic message from the SDK's error/response shape.

### JSON-Patch/RFC 6902 update helpers

- If the vendor's update API is a generic patch format (e.g. [JSON Patch/RFC 6902](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6902)) with a discriminated-union "value" wrapper type, a small set of shared helpers to build patch operations from typed structs (via a JSON round-trip through a plain map, if the wrapper type doesn't accept typed structs directly) tends to generalize well across every attribute on every target using the same update mechanism. **When one such patch op targets an attribute whose value the API itself enriches beyond what the practitioner configured** (see the "read-back enrichment" pattern below), do not include that op unconditionally on every `Update` call regardless of whether the attribute actually changed - only include it when the plan's value differs from the last-read state's value. Including it unconditionally risks resending only the practitioner's narrower configured subset (since state deliberately preserves the configured value, not the API's enriched one) and can trigger a confusing, seemingly-unrelated validation error server-side (e.g. rejecting the whole patch over a *different*, computed-only field that was never touched) purely because the enriched attribute's shape changed relative to its live value - confirmed live on one such attribute in this repo.

### "Read-back enrichment" pattern

- **"Read-back enrichment" pattern**: some vendor APIs merge additional server/connector-managed keys into a JSON-blob-shaped attribute the practitioner only partially configures (e.g. a "raw settings" map where the connector injects extra computed keys on `Read`). Preserve the practitioner's exact configured value in `dtoToModel` when it's known/configured (only falling back to the full API-returned value when Null/Unknown, e.g. post-import) - otherwise every `plan`/`apply` shows permanent phantom drift from the server's injected keys. See the point above for the corresponding `Update`-patch implication of this same pattern.

### Server-injected enrichment to a Required/Optional+Computed attribute (drift-blindness corollary)

- **A server-injected enrichment to a `Required` or `Optional+Computed` attribute cannot be echoed back into state at all if the attribute has a known config value - there is no schema-level escape hatch.** This is a stricter corollary of the "read-back enrichment" pattern above, discovered when the naive fixes for it were tried and both failed with distinct framework errors: (1) writing the API's enriched value into state for a plain `Required` attribute produces "Provider produced inconsistent result after apply" (a Required attribute's post-apply value must exactly equal the planned/configured value); (2) switching the attribute to `Optional: true, Computed: true` and adding a custom plan modifier that proposes `types.StringUnknown()`/equivalent whenever configured produces a *different*, harder error - "Provider produced invalid plan: planned value ... does not match config value ..." - because Terraform Core does not permit an Optional(+Computed) attribute to be planned Unknown when the practitioner's config sets a known, non-null value; only a pure Computed-only (non-Optional) attribute can diverge freely from config, or an Optional+Computed one whose config is null/unconfigured. The only correct fix: keep the attribute `Required` (or `Optional+Computed`) with no custom plan modifier, and in the response-to-model conversion, **never write the API's enriched value into state at all** - always keep the fallback (plan-on-Create/Update, prior-state-on-Read) value instead, documenting the resulting drift-blindness on that one field as a known limitation. A paired Computed-only data source for the same underlying object is unaffected by this and may freely reflect the true API-returned value, since a Computed-only attribute has no config value to conflict with.

### Pass-through-with-warning for unsupported-write attributes

- For attributes the provider doesn't yet have full write support for, prefer a "pass-through with an explicit warning diagnostic when configured" pattern over silently dropping the practitioner's configured value, and consider a deeper read-back (populating the attribute from the live API response) even without write support, so `plan`/`refresh` can still surface drift/defaults for that attribute.

### Plan modifier for computed-only server-managed scalars

- Any Computed-only, server-managed scalar attribute (e.g. an id or creation timestamp) that has no explicit spec-level default typically needs a hand-added plan modifier (e.g. "use prior state value when the proposed value would otherwise be Unknown") to avoid a permanent spurious diff, since most framework codegen tools do not emit plan modifiers themselves. Scope any such patch narrowly - do not apply an object/collection-level "use state for unknown" modifier to a block containing further nested Computed attributes with their own generated types, as this combination is known to break even a first-ever plan in at least one major codegen toolchain/version; prefer leaf-level (scalar) modifiers, and account for un-patched blocks via acceptance-test-level allowances instead.

### "Join"/membership sub-resource with no single-item CRUD

- **"Join"/membership sub-resource with no single-item CRUD**: some parent resources expose a collection sub-endpoint (e.g. group/team membership) shaped only as list + bulk-add + bulk-remove, with no get/patch/delete for a single member. This does not fit the standard per-item CRUD codegen assumption at all, so hand-write it as its own resource (not generated) that owns the *complete* desired set for one parent, keyed by the parent's id plus a set-valued attribute of member ids (parent id `Required`+`RequiresReplace`, member-set `Required`). Create/Update should diff current-vs-desired membership and call bulk-add/bulk-remove only for the deltas, treating a per-item "already present"/"already absent" error as satisfied rather than fatal (idempotent against out-of-band drift). Read should always re-list actual membership from the API rather than trust prior state verbatim, so `plan`/`refresh` self-heals if membership changed outside Terraform. Delete should bulk-remove every member tracked in state, treating a 404 on the parent itself (already gone) as a no-op. This is analogous to `aws_iam_group_membership`-style resources in other ecosystems - name it distinctly from the parent resource (e.g. `<parent>_members`) so both can coexist and be independently composed.

### Read-only sub-resource with no write endpoint at all

- **Read-only sub-resource with no write endpoint at all**: some parent resources expose a related collection that is entirely derived/read-only from the parent's perspective (e.g. "what other objects reference this one") with no create/update/delete operation anywhere in the spec - membership in that collection is instead established from the *other* object's own configuration. Do not model this as a resource (there is nothing to manage); model it as a plain hand-written data source (no generated counterpart, since there's no single-item CRUD shape to generate from) that lists/flattens the collection for one parent id. If the collection uses a different max page size than the parent's own list endpoint, do not assume they match - confirm each endpoint's documented/enforced limit independently.

### "Distributed" membership resource with no single collection endpoint at all

- **"Distributed" membership resource with no single collection endpoint at all**: a variant of the "Join" pattern above where there is no dedicated collection sub-endpoint for the association whatsoever - instead, membership is a plain attribute scattered across N *separate* parent objects of possibly different types (e.g. a "segment" attribute that lives on both a Role and an AccessProfile, each with its own independent get/patch endpoint). Model the association as its own resource exactly like the "Join" pattern (owns the complete desired member set for one parent-of-the-association, e.g. one segment's full list of {type, id} assignments), but implement Create/Update/Delete as an N-calls-per-apply loop: GET each individual member object, read its own membership-list attribute, add/remove only this resource's own key (preserving every other value already in that list - the member object can belong to multiple such associations simultaneously), then PATCH it back. Document the N+1-calls-per-apply cost as a known limitation. **Before designing this pattern at all, verify the "obvious" bulk/batch endpoint you may find via a spec-file grep is actually live** - see the dedicated Enforcement Rule below on spec-file presence not proving an endpoint is reachable; this exact pattern was only arrived at after a first design based on an unverified bulk endpoint failed entirely in live testing.

### Non-exclusive/partial association resource ("attach without owning the whole list")

- **Non-exclusive/partial association resource ("attach without owning the whole list")**: distinct from the "Join" pattern's *exclusive* full-membership ownership, some associations should only ever add/remove the specific members *this resource instance* configures, while always preserving any other members already attached to the same parent by some other means (another resource instance, a different tool, manual console action, etc.) - e.g. attaching a specific set of access-profile ids to an application that may already have others attached out-of-band. Implement Create as a union-merge (desired ids ∪ whatever's currently live, then write the union), Update as add-newly-configured/remove-newly-unconfigured but *only* for ids this resource's own prior state tracked (never touching ids the live object has that this resource never added), and Delete as removing only this resource's own tracked ids from the live list (leaving everything else the parent has untouched). This is the same category as e.g. `aws_iam_user_policy_attachment` (non-exclusive) as opposed to `aws_iam_group_membership` (exclusive) - always be explicit in the resource's own docs about which of the two semantics it implements, since practitioners commonly assume exclusive ownership by default.

### Optional+Computed field with no PlanModifier is reported Unknown (not Null) when omitted

- **Optional+Computed list-item field with no PlanModifier is reported Unknown (not Null) when omitted from config**: when a nested/list-item attribute is `Optional: true, Computed: true` with no `PlanModifier` (no `UseStateForUnknown`/`Default`), Terraform Core reports it as **Unknown** - not Null - during planning whenever a practitioner simply omits it from config, since the framework cannot statically know whether the provider computes a value for it. A hand-written model-to-API conversion function that only checks `field.IsNull()` before calling `.ValueString()`/equivalent is an incomplete guard: it will either error outright (if written defensively to reject Unknown) or silently misbehave, for the *normal, expected* case of a practitioner leaving an Optional field unset. Always check both `!field.IsNull() && !field.IsUnknown()` before reading such a field's value in a conversion function; treat Unknown the same as Null (omit from the request) when the field is purely practitioner-supplied with no real server-computed default, since a subsequent GET/PUT-response-driven Read always repopulates the true value afterward and this can never cause a "Provider produced inconsistent result after apply" error.

### "Adopt-existing" resource with no create/delete endpoint at all

- **"Adopt-existing" resource with no create/delete endpoint at all**: some resources represent objects that only ever come into existence as a side effect of some other process (e.g. sync/aggregation from an upstream system) and are never created or destroyed through the API being wrapped. Model `Create` as a *resolve*, not a POST: look the object up either directly by id, or via a filtered list/search on some natural key, and fail if not found; model `Delete` as a state-only `resp.State.RemoveResource(ctx)` with no API call (the object persists afterward - document this loudly in the resource's docs); model `Update` as a minimal patch over only the subset of fields the API actually documents as patchable, leaving everything else Computed-only. If the codegen tool requires a non-empty `create` operation even though there is none, point it at the same PATCH endpoint used for `Update` rather than the `Read` GET (pointing `create` at a GET can make some codegen tools silently skip generating the resource entirely with no error - watch for an expected resource missing from generated output, not just outright failures).

### Static spec-declared default doesn't match live API behavior

- **Static spec-declared default doesn't match live API behavior**: a schema `Default` in the OpenAPI spec is sometimes simply wrong relative to what the real API actually returns for that field (confirmed independently on multiple boolean/enum-with-a-declared-default fields across more than one target) - Phase B testing should specifically re-check every attribute with a spec-level `Default` against a real object's actual returned value, not just trust the spec, and strip/override the default in the code-spec/schema config if it's confirmed wrong rather than leaving a plan-time diff for practitioners to hit.

### Async (202-response + task-polling) write operations

- **Async (202-response + task-polling) write operations are a distinct pattern from every synchronous CRUD call**: some write endpoints return `202 Accepted` plus a reference to an async task/job rather than completing the change synchronously. Do not assume every operation on a target completes by the time its HTTP call returns - check the spec's declared response code before assuming synchronous semantics, and either poll the task to completion before returning from CRUD (if the practitioner needs to see the final state immediately) or explicitly document the async/eventually-consistent behavior as a known limitation if not polling.
